why: An FDE's output is mostly artifacts other people read without you in the room: the runbook the customer's on-call follows at 3am, the incident write-up their VP forwards to their CISO, the design doc that decides whether your integration ships. If the prose is vague, the deployment stalls in review; if it is precise, you buy trust you did not have to earn in a meeting. Public case studies do the same job pre-sales - a hiring loop or a prospect who has read three of your write-ups arrives already believing you can do the work, which is the single highest-leverage thing you can put on the internet in a job search.
prerequisites: At least three finished pieces of real work with a decision and a measurable outcome in them - ideally the Lumen FDE deployment, a migration or integration you owned, and a production incident you debugged end to end.
Working Git and Markdown: branches, PRs, fenced code blocks, and the docs-as-code idea from developer tooling and Git internals (topic 2).
Enough observability and SLO literacy (topics 27 and 29) to quote p50/p95/p99, error budgets and before/after numbers without hand-waving.
A publishing surface you control - rasul.in with a working build and deploy, plus the ability to add a route, an OG image and a feed.
Basic diagramming: you can draw a system as boxes with labelled arrows and know what a trust boundary is (threat modelling, topic 62).
Customer-facing judgement about what is confidential: contract terms, NDAs, and the difference between 'a fintech in Southeast Asia' and naming the account.

subtopics.name: Pick three stories that each contain a real decision
subtopics.learn: Before writing a word, list eight candidate stories from your own work and score each on: was there a decision with at least two defensible options, is there a number that moved, and can you publish it without leaking a customer. Keep the three that score highest and write one sentence per piece stating the reader ('a platform engineer evaluating whether to run this in their own VPC') and the one thing they should believe afterwards. Reject 'here is how I built a CRUD app' - a case study people share is one where the obvious answer was wrong and you show why. Write the three one-sentence promises down; every later cut is judged against them.

resource.label: Julia Evans - Some blogging myths (choosing what is worth publishing)

subtopics.name: The case-study spine: context, constraint, options, decision, mechanism, result
subtopics.learn: Adopt one skeleton and reuse it across all three pieces: (1) the situation and the hard constraint, (2) the two or three options actually on the table, (3) what you chose and the trade-off you accepted, (4) how the thing actually works, at the level of config keys and API calls, (5) what changed, with numbers, and (6) what you would do differently. This is the Architecture Decision Record shape (context / decision / consequences) stretched to narrative length. Draft all three spines as bullet outlines first and confirm each has a real 'consequences' section - the honest cost you paid is what makes readers trust the rest.

subtopics.name: Audience definition and the prerequisite contract
subtopics.learn: Work Google Technical Writing One's audience unit and apply it literally: write the reader's role, what they already know, and what they need to do after reading. Then compute the curse-of-knowledge delta - list every term you used that the reader does not have (IRSA, backpressure, idempotency key, ANN recall) and decide for each whether to define it inline, link it, or cut the sentence. State prerequisites explicitly at the top of a how-to ('assumes kubectl access and a namespace you can create Secrets in'). A reader who bounces at paragraph three because you assumed too much never tells you why.

subtopics.name: Sentence-level surgery: active voice, one idea, no zombie nouns
subtopics.learn: Run a mechanical pass over your draft: find every passive construction (search for 'was', 'were', 'is being', 'by the') and name the actor or justify keeping it; split any sentence over roughly 25 words; convert nominalisations back into verbs ('performed an evaluation of' becomes 'evaluated'); delete 'in order to', 'it should be noted that', 'basically', 'simply', 'just', 'obviously'. Replace vague quantifiers with numbers: 'significantly faster' becomes 'p95 fell from 4.1s to 380ms'. Do this as a timed pass, not while drafting - drafting and editing in the same pass is how people produce 3000 words that say nothing.

subtopics.name: Paragraphs, lists, tables, and summary-first structure
subtopics.learn: Apply Technical Writing Two's structural moves: one topic per paragraph with the point in the first sentence, three to five sentences max, and a hard rule that a reader skimming only your first sentences still gets the argument. Convert any sequence of 'and then' prose into a numbered list when order matters and a bulleted list when it does not; keep list items grammatically parallel. Convert any comparison of three or more things across two or more attributes into a table with the decision criterion as a column. Put the conclusion at the top of each section - technical readers scan, they do not read in order.

subtopics.name: Terminology discipline and a project word list
subtopics.learn: Pick one term per concept and never vary it for elegance - 'job' and 'task' and 'run' meaning the same thing across three sections is a bug, not style. Build a five-to-fifteen line word list at the top of your notes fixing your spellings and capitalisation (Kubernetes not k8s in prose, PostgreSQL not Postgres in headings, 'command-line' adjectival, 'sign in' verb vs 'sign-in' noun) and check it against Google's word list for the entries you are unsure about. Ban 'easy', 'simple', 'just' and 'obviously' outright: they tell a stuck reader the failure is theirs.

resource.label: Google developer documentation style guide - word list

subtopics.name: Diataxis: never blend tutorial, how-to, reference and explanation
subtopics.learn: Learn the four modes and their failure signature: a tutorial that stops to explain CAP theorem loses the beginner; a how-to that narrates your journey wastes an expert's time; reference that editorialises becomes untrustworthy; explanation with copy-paste commands gets pasted into production. Classify each of your three pieces (a case study is mostly explanation with a how-to appendix) and move any misplaced content out into a linked companion page. Apply the same test to the customer-facing docs you ship: if your runbook has a paragraph starting 'historically we...', it belongs somewhere else.

resource.label: Diataxis - the four kinds of documentation

subtopics.name: Blameless incident write-ups that survive a customer's exec reading them
subtopics.learn: Learn the postmortem template shape: impact stated in customer terms and duration, a timestamped timeline with timezone, root cause separated from triggering condition, what went well / what went badly / where we got lucky, and action items each with an owner, a due date and a type (prevent, detect, mitigate). Write in the passive-free but person-free register: 'the deploy script applied the migration before draining connections', never 'Priya forgot to drain connections'. Include the detection gap explicitly - how long between impact starting and anyone knowing - because that is the number that decides whether the customer trusts your monitoring.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

subtopics.name: Read five real published postmortems and steal their moves
subtopics.learn: Pick five write-ups from the post-mortems collection spanning different failure classes (cascading failure, config push, capacity exhaustion, data loss, dependency outage) and for each, annotate: how many sentences before you know the impact, where the timeline starts, how they describe the contributing cause without blame, and what they chose not to disclose. Notice that the widely-shared ones are specific and slightly uncomfortable - they name the wrong assumption. Extract three concrete devices (an impact box at the top, a 'why our monitoring missed it' section, a diagram of the request path at failure) and put them in your own template.

subtopics.name: Numbers that survive scrutiny: baselines, percentiles, and honest deltas
subtopics.learn: Every performance or cost claim needs four things stated: the baseline configuration, the measurement method and sample size, the percentile (never a bare average for latency), and the confounders you did not control. Write 'p99 ingest latency over 7 days of production traffic, ~2.1M requests/day, fell from 3.4s to 610ms after switching to batched upserts; hardware and traffic mix unchanged' rather than '5x faster'. Frame reliability numbers against an SLO and error budget rather than as raw uptime. If a number came from a synthetic benchmark, say so in the same sentence - a reader who catches you inflating one figure discounts the whole piece.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives

subtopics.name: One diagram per idea: C4 levels and drawing the trust boundary
subtopics.learn: Learn the C4 levels (system context, container, component, code) and pick exactly one level per diagram - the most common diagram failure is mixing a Kubernetes Pod, an AWS account boundary and a Python class in one picture. For a case study, a system-context diagram plus one container diagram is usually the whole visual budget. Label every arrow with protocol and direction of initiation ('HTTPS, service to API, mTLS'), draw the customer/vendor boundary explicitly, and give the diagram a caption that states its claim rather than its contents. Any diagram you cannot summarise in one sentence is two diagrams.

resource.label: The C4 model for visualising software architecture

subtopics.name: Diagrams as code, versioned next to the prose
subtopics.learn: Author diagrams in Mermaid (flowchart, sequenceDiagram, and the state and ER types) inside fenced ```mermaid blocks so they live in the same repo and PR as the text and never drift from it. Learn enough syntax to draw a request path with participants and activation bars, and a deployment topology with subgraphs for the VPC and cluster. Know the limits - once you need precise layout or annotation, export a hand-drawn SVG instead and commit the source file. Check that your site's renderer actually supports Mermaid before you commit to it; if not, render to SVG at build time.

resource.label: Mermaid docs - flowchart syntax (nodes, edges, subgraphs)

subtopics.name: Alt text, contrast, and images that survive dark mode
subtopics.learn: Write alt text that carries the informational content, not the filename: for a diagram, one sentence stating what it shows plus a pointer to the nearby prose that describes it fully; for decorative images, alt="" so screen readers skip them. Never put load-bearing information only in a screenshot - a terminal screenshot cannot be copied, searched, or read aloud, so paste the text too. Check contrast on diagram strokes and make sure exported PNGs with transparent backgrounds do not vanish on a dark-themed page; a flat background colour on the export is the cheap fix.

resource.label: W3C WAI - Images Tutorial (alt text decision tree)

subtopics.name: Code blocks and terminal transcripts that actually run
subtopics.learn: Every command you publish should be copy-pasteable: no leading '$' inside the copyable region, placeholders in an obvious form like <CLUSTER_NAME>, language tags on fences for highlighting, and long flags (--namespace not -n) so the reader can tell what they are running. Show the expected output right after the command so a reader can tell whether it worked. For multi-step flows, record an asciinema cast rather than a GIF - it is text, it is copyable, and it does not weigh 8MB. Before publishing, run every command in the piece on a clean machine or container; stale snippets are the number-one reason a technical post gets a scathing comment.

subtopics.name: Confidentiality: anonymise the customer, get approval, pick a licence
subtopics.learn: Establish a repeatable clearance loop: draft, strip identifying details (company name, headcount, exact ARR, cluster names, region if unusual, screenshots with hostnames and email addresses in them), replace with a category ('a Series-B logistics platform running ~200 services'), then send to your customer contact and get written approval before publishing - email is enough, verbal is not. Check the MSA/NDA for a publicity clause first. Redact credentials properly: rotate anything that appears in a screenshot rather than blurring it, and scrub .git history if a secret ever landed in the repo. Put an explicit licence on your own sample code so readers know they may use it.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Removing sensitive data from a repository

subtopics.name: Publishing mechanics on rasul.in: title, canonical URL, cards, dates
subtopics.learn: Ship each piece with: a title that states the specific claim ('Cutting p99 retrieval latency 5x by moving reranking off the request path' beats 'Lessons from an AI deployment'), a one-paragraph TL;DR above the fold, a stable slug you will never change, a canonical link tag, published and updated dates, and Open Graph plus Twitter card tags with a real og:image so the link renders as a card in Slack and LinkedIn instead of a bare URL. Test the card render with the platform's own debugger before you share. Confirm the page is server-rendered or statically generated so crawlers and link unfurlers see the text.

resource.label: Google Search Central - Canonical URLs and consolidating duplicate URLs

subtopics.name: Prose CI: Vale, markdownlint, and link checking in the build
subtopics.learn: Treat prose like code. Add markdownlint for structural rules (heading increments, fence languages, no trailing whitespace, line length) and Vale with a style based on the Google developer style guide plus a repo vocabulary file for your own terms and product names. Wire both into a GitHub Actions job on pull requests so a broken heading level or a banned word ('simply') fails the check before it ships. Add a link checker for internal and external links and run it on a schedule, not just on push, so rot in old posts surfaces. Set Vale's error/warning/suggestion levels deliberately - if everything is an error, you will disable it in a week.

subtopics.name: Ship, distribute, and handle the comment thread
subtopics.learn: Publishing is not distribution. For each piece: post to the two or three places your reader actually is, use the original title rather than editorialised bait, and be present for the first few hours to answer questions. Read the venue's rules before posting - most technical forums penalise self-promotional framing and reward a plain descriptive title and an author who replies substantively. When someone finds a genuine error, fix the post, add a dated correction note at the bottom, and thank them in the thread; when someone is just hostile, do not reply. Track which piece got forwarded internally by strangers - that, not raw traffic, is the signal the write-up worked.

outcomes: You can take a 2000-word draft and cut it 30% in one editing pass without losing a claim, showing the before/after word count and a list of the passive constructions, nominalisations and vague quantifiers you replaced.
You can state, for any page you write, which Diataxis mode it is and what belongs on a different page - and you can point at content you actually moved out.

You can write an incident write-up with impact in customer terms, a timestamped timeline with timezone, root cause separated from trigger, a stated detection gap, and action items that each have an owner, a date and a prevent/detect/mitigate label.
You can defend every number in your write-up: baseline, measurement method, sample size, percentile, and the confounders you did not control.

You can produce a system-context and a container diagram at a single C4 level each, authored as Mermaid in the repo, with protocol-labelled arrows, an explicit trust boundary and alt text that carries the content.
You can run every command in a published post on a clean container and have them all work, with expected output shown inline.
You can run a customer-clearance pass that strips identifying details, rotates any exposed credential, and produces written approval before publish.
You have three case studies live on rasul.in with canonical URLs, OG cards that render in Slack, a feed, and a CI job that lints prose and checks links on every pull request.
failureModes: The write-up leads with the journey ('when we first kicked off the project...') and buries impact and outcome under 800 words, so the exec who was forwarded it closes the tab before learning what happened.

A runbook says 'simply restart the service' with no expected output and no failure branch, so the customer's on-call at 3am runs it, sees an unfamiliar error, and escalates to you anyway - the doc bought nothing.
A screenshot in a published post contains a hostname, an internal email address or a partially visible token, and the account's security team finds it before you do.
Commands in the post were written from memory or from a shell with unexported env vars already set, so they fail for every reader on a clean machine and the top comment is someone pasting the error.

An incident report names an individual or a team as the cause, the customer's manager reads it, and the next incident gets reported to you late or not at all because people learned that honesty is punished.

Performance claims quote an average instead of a percentile and omit the baseline, so a sceptical engineer in the customer's review reproduces a different result and the whole document loses credibility.

Diagrams live in a Figma or Lucidchart file outside the repo, drift from the deployed architecture within two sprints, and are then used by a new joiner to reason about a system that no longer exists.
interviewQuestions: Walk me through a write-up you published about your own work. What did you cut, and how did you decide what was safe to disclose about the customer?

You have 45 minutes to write the customer-facing incident summary for a 4-hour partial outage in the integration you deployed. What sections do you write, in what order, and what do you deliberately leave out of the first version?

A customer's on-call engineer has to run your failover procedure for the first time at 3am with no context. Write - out loud - the first five lines of that runbook, and tell me what makes them safe to follow.
Your post claims a 5x latency improvement. I'm the skeptical staff engineer in the room. Convince me the number is real.
How do you decide whether something belongs in a tutorial, a how-to, reference, or an explanation page - and give me an example of a doc you've seen that failed because it mixed two of them.
You wrote a design doc, three reviewers left conflicting comments, and one of them is the customer's architect who outranks the others. How do you converge the document without a meeting?

We want our FDEs publishing customer case studies. Design the process end to end: what gets written, who reviews it, what the legal and confidentiality gates are, and how you keep it from becoming marketing fluff.
proofOfWork: Beyond the three published case studies, build and open-source a 'write-up kit' repo that turns your process into something another engineer can adopt in an afternoon. It contains four Markdown templates (case study, incident postmortem, design doc / ADR, and customer runbook) with inline commentary explaining what each section is for and the failure it prevents; a Vale style package with a vocabulary file plus a rules set that flags banned hedges ('simply', 'just', 'obviously'), bare averages for latency, undefined acronyms and passive-voice hot spots; a markdownlint config and a GitHub Actions workflow that runs both plus a link checker on every pull request; a redaction and clearance checklist covering screenshot scrubbing, credential rotation, git-history scanning and the written-approval step; and a short README that links each of your three published pieces to the template it was built from. Prove it works, not just that it exists: include the CI run on your own posts, a before/after diff of one draft showing the word count drop and the specific lint findings you fixed, and one piece of evidence that a real reader acted on the writing - a forwarded thread, an issue someone opened against your snippets, or a customer sign-off email (redacted) approving publication.
